danish.title: Ottende bog (1811–12) — Kapitel 2
paragraphs: I begyndelsen af vinteren flyttede fyrst Nikolaj Bolkonskij og hans datter til Moskva. På det tidspunkt var begejstringen for kejser Alexanders styre aftaget, og en patriotisk og franskfjendtlig stemning herskede, og dette, sammen med hans fortid og hans begavelse og hans egenart, gjorde straks fyrst Nikolaj Bolkonskij til genstand for særlig respekt blandt moskovitterne og til centrum for Moskvas opposition mod regeringen.

Fyrsten var ældet meget det år. Han viste tydelige tegn på alderdomssvækkelse med en tilbøjelighed til at falde i søvn, glemsomhed over for helt nylige begivenheder, erindring af fjerne, og den barnagtige forfængelighed, hvormed han accepterede rollen som leder af Moskvas opposition. Trods dette indgød den gamle mand alle sine besøgende en ærbødig ærefrygt — især om aftenen, når han kom ind til te i sin gammeldags frakke og puddrede paryk og, provokeret af nogen, fortalte sine bratte historier fra fortiden eller kom med endnu mere bratte og bidende kommentarer om nutiden. For dem alle frembød det gamle hus med dets kæmpemæssige spejle, førrevolutionære møbler, puddrede tjenere og den strenge, kloge gamle mand (selv et levn fra forrige århundrede) med sin milde datter og den smukke franskmand, der var hengivent knyttet til ham, et majestætisk og behageligt skue. Men gæsterne betænkte ikke, at udover de par timer, de så deres vært, var der også toogtyve timer i døgnet, hvor husets private og intime liv fortsatte.

Det private liv var i den senere tid blevet meget prøvende for fyrstinde Marja. I Moskva var hun berøvet sine største glæder — samtalerne med pilgrimme og den ensomhed, der forfriskede hende på Lysehøje — og hun havde ingen af bylivets fordele og fornøjelser. Hun kom ikke ud i selskabet; alle vidste, at hendes far ikke lod hende gå nogen steder uden ham, og hans svækkede helbred forhindrede ham i at gå ud selv, så hun ikke blev inviteret til middage og selskaber. Hun havde helt opgivet håbet om at blive gift. Hun så den kulde og ondsindethed, hvormed den gamle fyrste modtog og afviste de unge mænd, mulige friere, der ind imellem dukkede op i deres hus. Hun havde ingen venner: under dette besøg i Moskva var hun blevet skuffet over de to, der havde stået hende nærmest. Mademoiselle Bourienne, som hun aldrig havde kunnet være helt åbenhjertig over for, var nu blevet hende ubehagelig, og af forskellige grunde undgik fyrstinde Marja hende. Julie (Karagina), som hun havde brevvekslet med de sidste fem år, var i Moskva, men viste sig at være hende helt fremmed, da de mødtes. Netop da var Julie, der ved sine brødres død var blevet en af Moskvas rigeste arvinger, midt i selskabslivets hvirvel. Hun var omgivet af unge mænd, der, som hun indbildte sig, pludselig havde lært at sætte pris på hende. Julie befandt sig på det stadie i en selskabskvindes liv, hvor hun føler, at hendes sidste chance for at gifte sig er kommet, og at hendes skæbne må afgøres nu eller aldrig. Om torsdagen huskede fyrstinde Marja med et vemodigt smil, at hun nu ikke havde nogen at skrive til, da Julie — hvis nærvær ikke glædede hende — var her, og de sås hver uge. Ligesom den gamle emigrant, der afslog at gifte sig med den dame, han havde tilbragt sine aftener med i årevis, savnede hun Julies tilstedeværelse og at have nogen at skrive til. I Moskva havde fyrstinde Marja ingen at tale med, ingen at betro sin sorg, og der faldt megen sorg i hendes lod netop da. Tiden for fyrst Andrejs hjemkomst og bryllup nærmede sig, men hans anmodning til hende om at forberede faderen derpå var ikke blevet udført; ja, det forekom som om sagerne stod ganske håbløst, for ved enhver omtale af den unge grevinde Rostova tabte den gamle fyrste (der i forvejen for det meste var i dårligt humør) beherskelsen. En anden sorg, der var kommet til for nylig, skyldtes de lektioner, hun gav sin seksårige nevø. Til sin forfærdelse opdagede hun i sit forhold til lille Nikolaj nogle af sin fars pirrelighed. Hvor ofte hun end sagde til sig selv, at hun ikke måtte blive irritabel, når hun underviste sin nevø, følte hun næsten hver gang, med pegepinden i hånden, mens hun sad og viste ham det franske alfabet, et så stærkt ønske om hurtigt og let at hælde sin viden over i barnet — som allerede var bange for, at tante når som helst kunne blive vred — at hun ved den mindste uopmærksomhed rystede, blev forfjamsket og ophidset, hævede stemmen, og undertiden greb ham i armen og satte ham i hjørnet. Når hun havde sat ham i hjørnet, begyndte hun selv at græde over sin grusomme, onde natur, og lille Nikolaj, der fulgte hendes eksempel, hulkede og kom, uden at have fået lov, ud af sit hjørne, hen til hende, trak hendes våde hænder fra ansigtet og trøstede hende. Men hvad der plagede fyrstinden mest af alt, var hendes fars pirrelighed, som altid var rettet mod hende og i den senere tid nærmede sig grusomhed. Havde han tvunget hende til at ligge i knæfald på gulvet hele natten, havde han slået hende eller ladet hende hente brænde eller vand, ville det aldrig være faldet hende ind at tænke, at hendes stilling var hård; men denne kærlige despot — desto grummere fordi han elskede hende og netop derfor pinte sig selv og hende — vidste, hvordan han ikke blot kunne såre og ydmyge hende med vilje, men vise hende, at alt altid var hendes skyld. I den senere tid havde han vist et nyt træk, der pinte fyrstinde Marja mere end alt andet; det var hans stadig stigende fortrolighed med mademoiselle Bourienne. Den tanke, der i det første øjeblik ved nyheden om sønnens planer var faldet ham ind som spøg — at hvis Andrej giftede sig, ville han selv gifte sig med Bourienne — havde tydeligvis behaget ham, og på det seneste havde han vedholdende, og som det forekom fyrstinde Marja blot for at fornærme hende, vist særlige kærtegn mod sin ledsagerske og udtrykt sin utilfredshed med datteren ved demonstrativ kærlighed til Bourienne.

En dag i Moskva i fyrstinde Marjas nærværelse (hun troede, hendes far gjorde det med vilje, når hun var til stede) kyssede den gamle fyrste mademoiselle Bouriennes hånd og trak hende til sig og omfavnede hende kærligt. Fyrstinde Marja rødmede og løb ud af stuen. Et par minutter efter kom mademoiselle Bourienne ind i fyrstinde Marjas værelse, smilende og med muntre bemærkninger i sin behagelige stemme. Fyrstinde Marja tørrede hastigt sine tårer, gik resolut hen til mademoiselle Bourienne og begyndte, tydeligvis ubevidst om hvad hun gjorde, at skrige ad franskmanden i ophidset hast med bristende stemme: »Det er forfærdeligt, lavt, umenneskeligt at udnytte svagheden...« Hun nåede ikke at gøre sætningen færdig. »Forlad mit værelse,« udbrød hun og brast i gråd.

Næste dag sagde fyrsten ikke et ord til sin datter, men hun bemærkede, at han ved middagen beordrede, at mademoiselle Bourienne skulle serveres først. Efter middagen, da tjeneren bragte kaffe og af vane begyndte med fyrstinden, blev fyrsten pludselig rasende, kastede sin stok efter Filip og gav øjeblikkeligt ordre til at udskrive ham til hæren.

»Han adlyder ikke... jeg har sagt det to gange... og han adlyder ikke! Hun er den første person i dette hus; hun er min bedste ven,« skreg fyrsten. »Og hvis du tillader dig,« råbte han i raseri og henvendte sig for første gang til fyrstinde Marja, »igen at glemme dig selv over for hende, som du vovede i går, vil jeg vise dig, hvem der er herre i dette hus. Gå! Lad mig ikke se dig; bed hende om tilgivelse!«
Fyrstinde Marja bad mademoiselle Bourienne om tilgivelse, og også sin far om tilgivelse for sig selv og for tjeneren Filip, der havde bedt om hendes mellemkomst.

I sådanne øjeblikke samledes noget i hendes sjæl, der lignede en selvopofringens stolthed. Og pludselig ville den far, hun havde fordømt, lede efter sine briller i hendes nærværelse og famle tæt ved dem uden at se dem, eller glemme noget, der lige var sket, eller tage et usikkert skridt med sine svækkede ben og vende sig for at se, om nogen havde bemærket hans svaghed, eller, det værste af alt, ved middagen, når der ikke var gæster til at opmuntre ham, pludselig falde i søvn, lade servietten falde og det rystende hoved synke ned over tallerkenen. »Han er gammel og svag, og jeg vover at fordømme ham!« tænkte hun i sådanne øjeblikke med en følelse af afsky mod sig selv.

english.title: Book Eight (1811 - 12) — Chapter 2
paragraphs: At the beginning of winter, Prince Nicholas Bolkonsky and his daughter moved to Moscow. At that time, enthusiasm for Emperor Alexander's regime had waned and a patriotic, anti-French sentiment prevailed. This, combined with the old prince's record, his intellect, and his eccentricity, immediately made Prince Nicholas Bolkonsky an object of particular respect among Muscovites and the center of Moscow's opposition to the government.

The prince had aged greatly that year. He showed unmistakable signs of senility: a tendency to fall asleep at odd moments, forgetfulness of recent events, sharp recall of distant ones, and the childish vanity with which he embraced the role of head of the Moscow opposition. Despite this, the old man inspired the same feeling of respectful awe in every visitor — especially in the evenings when he appeared for tea in his old-fashioned coat and powdered wig and, prompted by someone, would tell his brusque stories of the past or deliver even more brusque and scathing judgments of the present. For them all, that old-fashioned house with its huge mirrors, pre-Revolution furniture, powdered footmen, and the stern, shrewd old man — himself a relic of the past century — with his gentle daughter and the pretty Frenchwoman, both reverently devoted to him, presented a majestic and charming spectacle. But the visitors didn't consider that besides the couple of hours during which they saw their host, there were twenty-two other hours in the day when the private, intimate life of the household went on.

That private life had lately become very hard for Princess Mary. Here in Moscow she was deprived of her greatest comforts — her conversations with the pilgrims and the solitude that restored her at Bald Hills — and she had none of the advantages and pleasures of city life. She didn't go out in society; everyone knew her father wouldn't let her go anywhere without him, and his failing health prevented him from going out, so she wasn't invited to dinners or parties. She had completely given up hope of getting married. She saw the coldness and contempt with which the old prince received and dismissed the young men who sometimes appeared at their house as possible suitors. She had no friends: during this visit to Moscow she had been disappointed in the two people who had been closest to her. Mademoiselle Bourienne, with whom she had never been entirely open, had now become unpleasant to her, and for various reasons Princess Mary avoided her. Julie, with whom she had corresponded for five years, turned out to be completely alien when they met in person. Julie — who had become one of Moscow's wealthiest heiresses through the death of her brothers — was deep in the whirl of society pleasures. She was surrounded by young men who, she fancied, had suddenly learned to appreciate her worth. Julie was at that stage in a society woman's life when she feels that her last chance of marrying has come and her fate must be decided now or never. On Thursdays Princess Mary recalled with a sad smile that she now had no one to write to, since Julie — whose presence gave her no joy — was right here in Moscow, and they saw each other weekly. Like the old emigre who declined to marry the lady with whom he'd spent his evenings for years, she regretted Julie's presence and missed having someone to write to. In Moscow, Princess Mary had no one to talk to, no one to confide in — and much sorrow had recently fallen on her. The time for Prince Andrew's return and marriage was approaching, but his request that she prepare their father for it had not been carried out; in fact, things seemed quite hopeless — at every mention of the young Countess Rostova the old prince, who was usually in a bad temper anyway, lost all self-control. Another recent sorrow arose from the lessons she gave her six-year-old nephew. To her dismay she detected in herself, when dealing with little Nicholas, symptoms of her father's irritability. No matter how often she told herself she must not lose patience while teaching her nephew, almost every time she sat down with pointer in hand to show him the French alphabet, she so desperately wanted to pour her own knowledge quickly into the child — who was already afraid that Auntie might get angry at any moment — that at the slightest inattention she would tremble, become flustered and heated, raise her voice, and sometimes grab him by the arm and stand him in the corner. Having put him there she would cry over her own cruel, wicked nature, and little Nicholas, following her example, would sob, and without permission would leave his corner, come to her, pull her wet hands from her face, and comfort her. But what distressed the princess most of all was her father's irritability, which was always directed at her and had lately come close to cruelty. Had he forced her to prostrate herself on the ground all night, had he beaten her or made her haul firewood and water, it would never have entered her mind to think her lot was hard; but this loving tyrant — all the more cruel because he loved her and tormented himself on her account — knew how not merely to hurt and humiliate her deliberately, but to make her feel that she was always to blame for everything. Lately he had developed a new trait that tormented Princess Mary more than anything: his growing closeness to Mademoiselle Bourienne. The notion that had occurred to him as a joke when he first learned of his son's plans — that if Andrew married, he himself would marry Bourienne — had evidently pleased him, and lately he had been persistently, as it seemed to Princess Mary solely to wound her, showing the companion exaggerated affection and expressing displeasure with his daughter through demonstrations of love for Bourienne.

One day in Moscow, in Princess Mary's presence — she believed her father did it on purpose when she was there — the old prince kissed Mademoiselle Bourienne's hand and, pulling her close, embraced her tenderly. Princess Mary flushed and ran from the room. A few minutes later Mademoiselle Bourienne came into Princess Mary's room, smiling and chatting in her pleasant voice. Princess Mary quickly wiped away her tears, went resolutely up to Mademoiselle Bourienne, and — evidently unaware of what she was doing — began shouting in angry haste at the Frenchwoman, her voice breaking: "It's horrible, vile, inhuman — to take advantage of weakness..." She didn't finish. "Get out of my room," she cried, and burst into sobs.

The next day the prince didn't say a word to his daughter, but she noticed that at dinner he ordered Mademoiselle Bourienne to be served first. After dinner, when the footman brought the coffee and from habit started with the princess, the prince flew into a sudden rage, threw his stick at Philip the footman, and immediately gave orders for him to be sent into the army.

"He doesn't obey... I said it twice... and he doesn't obey! She is the first person in this house; she is my best friend," the prince shouted. "And if you allow yourself," he screamed, addressing Princess Mary for the first time, "to forget yourself again in her presence as you did yesterday, I will show you who is master in this house. Now go! And don't let me see you again — beg her pardon!"
Princess Mary asked Mademoiselle Bourienne's forgiveness, and also her father's forgiveness for herself and for Philip the footman, who had begged her to intercede.

At such moments something like a pride of sacrifice gathered in her soul. And then suddenly that same father she had judged would begin groping for his spectacles in her presence, fumbling near them but not finding them, or would forget something that had just happened, or would take a false step with his failing legs and turn to see if anyone had noticed his weakness, or — worst of all — would suddenly fall asleep at dinner when there were no guests to stimulate him, letting his napkin slip and his trembling head droop over his plate. "He is old and feeble, and I dare to judge him!" she would think at such moments, with a wave of self-reproach.
